boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Lawrence record (August 21, 1863) in Quantrill's Raid into Kansas [August 1863]. The approach march of August 19-20, the pursuit through Paola to Grand River (August 21-22), later guerrilla deaths and Order No. 11 are context. Most of the dead were unarmed civilians; they are recorded as reported, not as ordinary combat casualties. Campaign-wide marches, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads No Union troops [US] and Quantrill's Raiders and other guerrillas [CS], with no numerical bounds; the live field reads 350 (US 0; CS 350) and the live description says 300 to 400. Ewing says Quantrill's whole force was about 300, about 250 assembling first and about 50 joining on the 20th; Banks's dispatch estimates about 200. Britton says three hundred crossed into Kansas and that Pike's first report put them as high as seven hundred. Ewing says the people of Lawrence could have met Quantrill with 500 men on half an hour's notice, and that among the murdered were 14 recruits of the Fourteenth Kansas and 20 of the Second Kansas Colored.
claims.rationale: Estimates of an irregular force, and a counterfactual defence figure. The murdered recruits were unarmed, so the frozen 'No Union troops' is not contradicted as a count of an armed defence. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

Britton gives the same account.
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from an interested report and a history; no original messages inspected.

claims.rationale: Stated or attributed aims from a summary, a history and an interested report; no guerrilla account inspected.

claims.value: NPS says Quantrill led the force. Ewing, absent at Leavenworth, blames Pike's error of judgment in not pursuing at once and says Clark was slow to renew the pursuit; Plumb led the pursuit and Lane a party of citizens. Britton calls Pike's failure the first fatal blunder. The frozen commander is Lieutenant Colonel William C. Quantrill; no Union commander is listed, and the live page styles Quantrill a Colonel.
claims.rationale: Command roles from a summary, an interested report and a history; the listed commander does not receive automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Confederate victory and the live result Confederate Victory. Ewing says the guerrillas robbed most stores and banks, burned 185 buildings including a quarter of the private residences and nearly all business houses, and murdered 140 unarmed men; Britton says they held the town until ten o'clock. NPS calls it the extreme example of the border warfare.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The label records a raid on an undefended town, not a battle between armed forces.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 204 total (US 164; CS 40); the live field reads 150 (US 150; CS 0). Ewing says 140 unarmed men were murdered and about 24 persons wounded, and that the guerrillas killed since the raid already numbered fully a hundred; Banks's same-day dispatch says about 60 citizens (read 'GO') were slaughtered; Britton says 140 men were killed and 185 buildings burned.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Civilian dead are not military casualties; guerrillas killed in the pursuit and later scouts belong to separate actions and are not added.

open_questions: Schofield's transmittal (No. 1, read at its opening and not selected), Clark's, Lazear's, Thacher's, Coleman's, Ballinger's, Leland's and King's reports (Nos. 3-9), any guerrilla account and a list of the Lawrence dead remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Wiley Britton's The Civil War on the Border, volume II (Putnam's, 1899) is a retrospective history described on its title page as based upon official reports and the author's observations; it relays figures from Union and Confederate reports, so it is not independent of the Official Records families, and is treated as partly a participant's interested Union account. Ewing's August 31, 1863 report is one family of interested Union accounts; A. R. Banks's August 21 dispatch from Lawrence, printed as its inclosure, is a separate writer's dispatch not counted as a further family. No Confederate or guerrilla account of the raid was located in the inspected volume. Official Records Series I, Volume XXII, Part 1 is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
